description: Question bank extracted from Plate Tectonics PDF. Covers all syllabus points, definitions, classifications, examples, processes, comparison tables, India-focused facts, common exam traps and practice questions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the theory of plate tectonics?

options.A: The theory that continents are fixed and do not move
options.B: The scientific theory that Earth's rigid outer shell, the lithosphere, is divided into plates that move relative to one another over the ductile asthenosphere
options.C: The theory that the Earth's core is liquid and drives magnetic fields
options.D: The theory that the ocean floor is permanently fixed and unchanging

questions.explanation: Plate tectonics is the scientific theory that Earth's rigid outer shell, the lithosphere, is divided into a number of large and small plates that move relative to one another over the ductile asthenosphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: At which boundaries do tectonic plates interact?

options.A: Only at divergent boundaries
options.B: Only at convergent boundaries
options.C: Through divergence, convergence and transform motion at their boundaries

questions.explanation: The plates interact at their boundaries through divergence, convergence and transform motion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What does a tectonic plate consist of?

options.A: Only continental crust
options.B: Only oceanic crust
options.C: Lithosphere, which may contain continental crust, oceanic crust, or both, together with the rigid uppermost mantle beneath the crust

questions.explanation: A tectonic plate consists of lithosphere. It may contain continental crust, oceanic crust, or both, together with the rigid uppermost mantle beneath the crust.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT explained by plate tectonics?

options.A: Seafloor spreading
options.B: Subduction
options.D: The origin of the Earth's magnetic field

questions.explanation: Plate tectonics explains the distribution and movement of continents and ocean basins, seafloor spreading, subduction, mountain building, ocean trenches, mid-ocean ridges, earthquakes, volcanic belts and many major geological structures. The origin of the Earth's magnetic field is explained by the geodynamo theory, not plate tectonics.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is plate tectonics different from continental drift?

options.A: Continental drift explains that entire lithospheric plates move, while plate tectonics argues that only continents move
options.B: Continental drift, proposed by Alfred Wegener, argued that continents move but did not provide an adequate mechanism; plate tectonics explains that entire lithospheric plates move, carrying both continents and ocean floors, and describes how plates interact and recycle oceanic lithosphere
options.C: Continental drift was proposed in the 1960s, while plate tectonics was proposed in 1912
options.D: There is no difference between the two theories

questions.explanation: Continental drift, proposed by Alfred Wegener, argued that continents move but did not provide an adequate mechanism. Plate tectonics explains that entire lithospheric plates move, carrying both continents and ocean floors, and describes how plates interact and recycle oceanic lithosphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: When did plate tectonics become widely accepted?

options.A: In the 1910s
options.B: In the 1940s

questions.explanation: The modern theory developed mainly during the 1960s, following advances in ocean-floor mapping, palaeomagnetism, earthquake studies and the seafloor-spreading hypothesis.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Who proposed continental drift?

options.A: Harry Hess
options.B: Alfred Wegener

questions.explanation: Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Who discussed mantle convection as a possible driver of plate motion?

options.A: Alfred Wegener
options.B: Harry Hess

questions.explanation: Arthur Holmes discussed mantle convection as a possible driver.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Who developed the seafloor-spreading hypothesis?

options.A: Alfred Wegener
options.B: Harry Hess

questions.explanation: Harry Hess developed the seafloor-spreading hypothesis.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What did the Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis explain?

options.A: The origin of continents
options.B: Magnetic stripes as evidence of seafloor spreading
options.D: The cause of earthquakes at transform boundaries

questions.explanation: The Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis explained magnetic stripes as evidence of spreading.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the lithosphere?

options.A: Earth's strong, rigid outer shell consisting of the crust and the rigid uppermost part of the mantle, broken into tectonic plates
options.B: A weak, ductile region of the upper mantle

questions.explanation: The lithosphere is Earth's strong, rigid outer shell. It consists of the crust and the rigid uppermost part of the mantle. It is broken into tectonic plates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the asthenosphere?

options.A: A completely liquid global ocean of magma
options.B: A relatively weak and ductile region of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere, predominantly solid rock that can deform and flow slowly over geological time
options.C: The outermost compositional layer of the Earth
options.D: The rigid uppermost mantle attached to the crust

questions.explanation: The asthenosphere is a relatively weak and ductile region of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere. It is predominantly solid rock that can deform and flow slowly over geological time; it is not a global ocean of liquid magma.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the difference between crust and lithosphere?

options.A: The crust includes the lithosphere
options.B: The crust is Earth's outermost compositional layer; the lithosphere includes the crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle, making it thicker and defined by mechanical behaviour rather than composition alone
options.D: The lithosphere is composed only of oceanic crust

questions.explanation: The crust is Earth's outermost compositional layer. The lithosphere includes the crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle. Therefore, lithosphere is thicker than crust and is defined by mechanical behaviour rather than composition alone.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the two main types of crust?

options.A: Lithospheric and asthenospheric crust
options.B: Continental crust and oceanic crust

questions.explanation: The two main types of crust are continental crust and oceanic crust.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes continental crust?

options.A: Generally thinner, denser and mainly basaltic to gabbroic
options.B: Generally thicker, less dense and compositionally more varied, commonly rich in granitic rocks
options.D: The same density as oceanic crust

questions.explanation: Continental crust is generally thicker, less dense and compositionally more varied, commonly rich in granitic rocks.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes oceanic crust?

options.A: Generally thicker and less dense, rich in granitic rocks
options.B: Generally thinner, denser and mainly basaltic to gabbroic
options.D: The same thickness as continental crust

questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is generally thinner, denser and mainly basaltic to gabbroic.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why do oceanic plates commonly subduct beneath continental plates?

options.A: Because oceanic plates are less dense than continental plates
options.B: Because oceanic lithosphere is generally denser than continental lithosphere, especially as it cools and becomes older
options.C: Because continental plates are always moving faster

questions.explanation: Oceanic lithosphere is generally denser than continental lithosphere, especially as it cools and becomes older. At many convergent boundaries, the denser oceanic plate descends into the mantle beneath the more buoyant continental plate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which layer forms the upper part of the lithosphere?

options.A: The asthenosphere
options.B: The crust (continental or oceanic)

questions.explanation: The crust forms the upper part of the lithosphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the role of the asthenosphere in plate tectonics?

options.A: It forms the rigid outer shell divided into plates
options.B: It allows long-term movement and deformation of the lithosphere
options.C: It is the source of the Earth's magnetic field
options.D: It is the layer where earthquakes originate

questions.explanation: The asthenosphere is a weak, ductile upper-mantle region that allows long-term movement and deformation of the lithosphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the deeper mantle in the context of plate tectonics?

options.A: It is completely liquid and does not convect
options.B: It is solid rock that convects over geological time and is part of the thermal and dynamic system influencing plate motion
options.C: It is the same as the asthenosphere
options.D: It plays no role in plate motion

questions.explanation: The deeper mantle is solid rock that convects over geological time and is part of the thermal and dynamic system influencing plate motion.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are lithospheric plates?

options.A: Large, relatively rigid sections of Earth's lithosphere that move slowly over geological time
options.B: Liquid layers of the outer core
options.C: Regions of the asthenosphere that do not move
options.D: Parts of the crust that are permanently fixed

questions.explanation: Lithospheric plates are large, relatively rigid sections of Earth's lithosphere that move slowly over geological time. Their boundaries are zones where most plate-related earthquakes, volcanoes and major deformation occur.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How fast do tectonic plates move?

options.A: Several metres per year
options.B: A few millimetres to several centimetres per year
options.D: They do not move at all

questions.explanation: Most plates move at rates of a few millimetres to several centimetres per year. Rates vary by plate and location; some oceanic plates move at several centimetres per year.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Do plates move over a liquid mantle?

options.A: Yes, the asthenosphere is a global ocean of liquid magma
options.B: No, the asthenosphere is mostly solid but behaves ductilely over long periods; plate motion occurs through deformation and flow of solid mantle materials
options.C: Yes, the entire mantle is liquid
options.D: No, plates float on the liquid outer core

questions.explanation: No. The asthenosphere is mostly solid but behaves ductilely over long periods. Plate motion occurs through deformation and flow of solid mantle materials.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which forces contribute to plate motion?

options.A: Only tidal forces
options.B: Slab pull, ridge push and tractions associated with mantle flow
options.D: Only gravitational attraction of the Moon

questions.explanation: Important forces include slab pull, ridge push and tractions associated with mantle flow. Slab pull is commonly considered a major driver in many regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is slab pull?

options.A: The force that pushes plates away from mid-ocean ridges
options.B: The force associated with a cold, dense oceanic plate sinking into the mantle at a subduction zone and pulling the rest of the plate behind it
options.C: The force of mantle convection pushing plates sideways
options.D: The frictional force between two transform plates

questions.explanation: Slab pull is the force associated with a cold, dense oceanic plate sinking into the mantle at a subduction zone and pulling the rest of the plate behind it.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is ridge push?

options.A: The force associated with a sinking slab
options.B: The gravitational force component that tends to move lithosphere away from the elevated mid-ocean ridge towards lower elevations
options.C: The force that pulls plates together at convergent boundaries
options.D: The force that causes earthquakes at transform boundaries

questions.explanation: Ridge push is the gravitational force component that tends to move lithosphere away from the elevated mid-ocean ridge towards lower elevations.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What role does mantle convection play in plate tectonics?

options.A: It has no role
options.B: Heat-driven mantle circulation contributes to the dynamic environment in which plates move; mantle flow and plate motion interact
options.C: It is the sole mechanism of plate motion

questions.explanation: Heat-driven mantle circulation contributes to the dynamic environment in which plates move. Mantle flow and plate motion interact; simple textbook diagrams of convection cells are useful models but do not capture every detail of real mantle dynamics.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the commonly taught list of seven major tectonic plates?

options.A: Pacific, North American, South American, African, Eurasian, Antarctic and Indo-Australian
options.B: Pacific, Nazca, Cocos, Caribbean, Arabian, Scotia and Juan de Fuca
options.C: African, Eurasian, Antarctic, Nazca, Cocos, Caribbean and Philippine Sea
options.D: North American, South American, African, Eurasian, Antarctic, Arabian and Somali

questions.explanation: A commonly taught list of seven major plates is the Pacific, North American, South American, African, Eurasian, Antarctic and Indo-Australian plates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the largest tectonic plate?

options.A: Eurasian Plate
options.B: African Plate

questions.explanation: The Pacific Plate is the largest tectonic plate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which plate includes most of the Indian subcontinent?

options.A: Eurasian Plate
options.B: Indian Plate

questions.explanation: The Indian Plate includes most of the Indian subcontinent. In some simplified school-level diagrams, it is included within the combined Indo-Australian Plate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Is the Indo-Australian Plate always treated as one plate?

options.A: Yes, it is always treated as a single plate in all models
options.B: No, many introductory diagrams use the Indo-Australian Plate as a single major plate, but geophysical evidence and modern models often distinguish the Indian Plate and Australian Plate, with a broad and complex deformation zone between them
options.C: Yes, because India and Australia move at exactly the same rate
options.D: No, because the Indo-Australian Plate does not exist

questions.explanation: No. Many introductory diagrams use the Indo-Australian Plate as a single major plate, but geophysical evidence and modern models often distinguish the Indian Plate and Australian Plate, with a broad and complex deformation zone between them.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the significance of the Pacific Plate?

options.A: It is the smallest plate and has no active boundaries
options.B: It is the largest plate and is surrounded by many active plate boundaries, including subduction zones that contribute to the circum-Pacific earthquake and volcanic belt known as the Ring of Fire
options.D: It is located entirely in the Atlantic Ocean

questions.explanation: The Pacific Plate is the largest plate and is surrounded by many active plate boundaries, including subduction zones that contribute to the circum-Pacific earthquake and volcanic belt known as the Ring of Fire.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the North American Plate?

options.A: It includes North America, Greenland and adjacent oceanic lithosphere
options.B: It includes only the continent of North America
options.C: It is the largest tectonic plate

questions.explanation: The North American Plate includes North America, Greenland and adjacent oceanic lithosphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the South American Plate?

options.A: It includes South America and adjacent Atlantic oceanic lithosphere to the east
options.B: It includes only the continent of South America
options.D: It is the smallest major plate

questions.explanation: The South American Plate includes South America and adjacent Atlantic oceanic lithosphere to the east.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the African Plate?

options.A: It includes Africa and adjacent oceanic lithosphere
options.B: It includes only the continent of Africa
options.D: It is the largest tectonic plate

questions.explanation: The African Plate includes Africa and adjacent oceanic lithosphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the Eurasian Plate?

options.A: It includes only Europe
options.B: It includes most of Europe and much of Asia; boundaries are complex in the south and east
options.D: It is the smallest major plate

questions.explanation: The Eurasian Plate includes most of Europe and much of Asia; boundaries are complex in the south and east.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the Antarctic Plate?

options.A: It includes Antarctica and surrounding oceanic lithosphere
options.B: It includes only the continent of Antarctica
options.C: It is the largest tectonic plate

questions.explanation: The Antarctic Plate includes Antarctica and surrounding oceanic lithosphere.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the traditional combined label for the Indian and Australian plate regions?

options.A: Indo-Eurasian Plate
options.B: Indo-Australian Plate

questions.explanation: The Indo-Australian Plate is the traditional combined label for Indian and Australian plate regions; some models separate them.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are minor tectonic plates?

options.A: Plates that do not move
options.B: Smaller lithospheric plates compared with the major plates, which are nevertheless important because their boundaries can produce earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building and complex regional tectonics
options.C: Plates composed only of continental crust
options.D: Plates located only in the Atlantic Ocean

questions.explanation: Minor plates are smaller lithospheric plates compared with the major plates. They are nevertheless important because their boundaries can produce earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain building and complex regional tectonics.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a commonly shown minor tectonic plate?

options.A: Pacific Plate
options.B: Nazca Plate

questions.explanation: Examples commonly shown on tectonic maps include the Nazca, Cocos, Caribbean, Philippine Sea, Arabian, Scotia, Juan de Fuca and Somali plates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Nazca Plate located and what is its tectonic significance?

options.A: Off western South America; it subducts beneath the South American Plate and contributes to the Andes
options.B: Off Central America; it subducts beneath the Caribbean Plate
options.C: In the western Pacific; it is involved in island-arc systems

questions.explanation: The Nazca Plate is located off western South America; it subducts beneath the South American Plate and contributes to the Andes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Cocos Plate located and what is its tectonic significance?

options.A: Off western South America; it subducts beneath the South American Plate
options.B: Off Central America; it subducts beneath parts of the Caribbean and North American plate systems
options.C: In the western Pacific; it is involved in island-arc systems

questions.explanation: The Cocos Plate is located off Central America; it subducts beneath parts of the Caribbean and North American plate systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Caribbean Plate located and what is its tectonic significance?

options.A: Off western South America; it subducts beneath the South American Plate
options.B: In the Caribbean region; it interacts with North American and South American plates
options.C: In the western Pacific; it is involved in island-arc systems

questions.explanation: The Caribbean Plate is located in the Caribbean region; it interacts with North American and South American plates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Philippine Sea Plate located and what is its tectonic significance?

options.A: Off western South America; it subducts beneath the South American Plate
options.B: In the western Pacific; it is involved in complex subduction and island-arc systems
options.C: In the Caribbean region; it interacts with North American and South American plates

questions.explanation: The Philippine Sea Plate is located in the western Pacific; it is involved in complex subduction and island-arc systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Arabian Plate located and what is its tectonic significance?

options.A: Off western South America; it subducts beneath the South American Plate
options.B: In the Arabian Peninsula; it moves generally northward towards Eurasia
options.C: In the western Pacific; it is involved in island-arc systems

questions.explanation: The Arabian Plate is located in the Arabian Peninsula; it moves generally northward towards Eurasia.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Scotia Plate located and what is its tectonic significance?

options.A: Off western South America; it subducts beneath the South American Plate
options.B: Between the southern tip of South America and Antarctica
options.C: In the western Pacific; it is involved in island-arc systems
options.D: In the Arabian Peninsula; it moves northward towards Eurasia

questions.explanation: The Scotia Plate is located between the southern tip of South America and Antarctica.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Juan de Fuca Plate located and what is its tectonic significance?

options.A: Off western South America; it subducts beneath the South American Plate
options.B: Off the Pacific Northwest of North America; it subducts beneath the North American Plate
options.C: In the western Pacific; it is involved in island-arc systems

questions.explanation: The Juan de Fuca Plate is located off the Pacific Northwest of North America; it subducts beneath the North American Plate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Where is the Somali Plate located and what is its tectonic significance?

options.A: Off western South America; it subducts beneath the South American Plate
options.B: In the eastern part of Africa, separating from the Nubian part of the African Plate in the East African Rift system
options.C: In the western Pacific; it is involved in island-arc systems

questions.explanation: The Somali Plate is located in the eastern part of Africa, separating from the Nubian part of the African Plate in the East African Rift system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which plate is responsible for subduction beneath the western margin of South America?

options.A: Cocos Plate
options.B: Nazca Plate

questions.explanation: The Nazca Plate subducts beneath the South American Plate, contributing to the formation and uplift of the Andes and associated volcanism.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which plate is associated with the island-arc region east of the Philippines?

options.A: Nazca Plate
options.B: Philippine Sea Plate

questions.explanation: The Philippine Sea Plate is a key plate in the complex tectonic setting of the western Pacific, alongside the Philippine Mobile Belt and neighbouring plates.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a plate boundary?

options.A: The centre of a tectonic plate
options.B: A zone where two tectonic plates meet and interact
options.C: The boundary between the crust and the mantle
options.D: The boundary between the lithosphere and the asthenosphere

questions.explanation: A plate boundary is a zone where two tectonic plates meet and interact. The three principal types are divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the three principal types of plate boundaries?

options.A: Divergent, convergent and transform
options.B: Ridge, trench and fault

questions.explanation: The three principal types are divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a divergent plate boundary?

options.A: A plate margin where two plates move towards each other
options.B: A plate margin where two lithospheric plates move away from each other; mantle material rises to fill the gap and decompression melting can produce magma that cools to form new oceanic crust
options.C: A plate margin where two plates slide horizontally past each other
options.D: A zone where oceanic lithosphere descends into the mantle

questions.explanation: A divergent boundary is a plate margin where two lithospheric plates move away from each other. Mantle material rises to fill the gap; decompression melting can produce magma that cools to form new oceanic crust.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What landforms are produced at divergent boundaries?

options.A: Ocean trenches and volcanic arcs
options.B: Mid-ocean ridges in oceanic settings and rift valleys in continental settings

questions.explanation: Mid-ocean ridges in oceanic settings and rift valleys in continental settings. Volcanism and shallow earthquakes are also common.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a major oceanic example of a divergent boundary?

options.A: San Andreas Fault
options.B: Mid-Atlantic Ridge

questions.explanation: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a major oceanic example. The East African Rift is an important continental rift system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is an important continental rift system?

options.A: Mid-Atlantic Ridge
options.B: East African Rift

questions.explanation: The East African Rift is an important continental rift system.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What happens when continental rifting continues?

options.A: The continental crust immediately becomes oceanic crust
options.B: The continental crust may thin and fracture, a rift valley may develop, and continued extension can eventually produce new oceanic crust and a widening ocean basin
options.C: The rift immediately closes and forms a mountain range

questions.explanation: The continental crust may thin and fracture, a rift valley may develop, and continued extension can eventually produce new oceanic crust and a widening ocean basin. This is a long-term process, not an instantaneous event.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What type of earthquakes are typical at divergent boundaries?

options.A: Deep-focus earthquakes only
options.B: Shallow earthquakes

questions.explanation: Divergent boundaries are associated with shallow earthquakes, basaltic volcanism, rifts and mid-ocean ridges.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What type of volcanism is typical at divergent boundaries?

options.A: Basaltic volcanism
options.B: Rhyolitic volcanism only

questions.explanation: Divergent boundaries are associated with basaltic volcanism.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a convergent plate boundary?

options.A: A plate margin where two plates move away from each other
options.B: A plate margin where two plates move towards each other; depending on the types of plates, convergence can cause subduction or continental collision
options.C: A plate margin where two plates slide horizontally past each other
options.D: A zone where new oceanic crust is created

questions.explanation: A convergent boundary is a plate margin where two plates move towards each other. Depending on the types of plates, convergence can cause subduction or continental collision.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the three common types of convergent boundary?

options.A: Divergent, transform and oblique
options.B: Oceanic-continental convergence, oceanic-oceanic convergence and continental-continental convergence

questions.explanation: The three common types of convergent boundary are oceanic-continental convergence, oceanic-oceanic convergence and continental-continental convergence.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What happens at an oceanic-continental convergent boundary?

options.A: The continental plate subducts beneath the oceanic plate
options.B: The denser oceanic plate commonly subducts beneath the continental plate; a deep ocean trench may form offshore, while earthquakes and magma generation can produce a volcanic mountain belt on the continent
options.C: Both plates slide past each other

questions.explanation: The denser oceanic plate commonly subducts beneath the continental plate. A deep ocean trench may form offshore, while earthquakes and magma generation can produce a volcanic mountain belt on the continent. The Andes are a classic example.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mountain range is a classic example of oceanic-continental convergence?

options.A: Himalayas
options.B: Andes

questions.explanation: The Andes are a classic example of oceanic-continental convergence, where the Nazca Plate subducts beneath the South American Plate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What happens at an oceanic-oceanic convergent boundary?

options.A: Both plates collide and form fold mountains
options.B: One oceanic plate commonly subducts beneath the other; a trench and a volcanic island arc may form
options.D: The plates slide past each other

questions.explanation: One oceanic plate commonly subducts beneath the other. A trench and a volcanic island arc may form. The western Pacific contains several examples of complex island-arc and subduction systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What happens at a continental-continental convergent boundary?

options.A: One continental plate subducts deeply beneath the other
options.B: After intervening oceanic lithosphere is consumed, two buoyant continental masses collide; the crust shortens, folds, faults and thickens, producing high mountain belts and elevated plateaus
options.D: The plates slide past each other

questions.explanation: After intervening oceanic lithosphere is consumed, two buoyant continental masses collide. The crust shortens, folds, faults and thickens, producing high mountain belts and elevated plateaus. The Himalayas are the classic example.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mountain range is a classic example of continental-continental convergence?

options.A: Andes
options.B: Himalayas

questions.explanation: The Himalayas are the classic example of continental-continental convergence.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are volcanoes always formed at convergent boundaries?

options.A: Yes, all convergent boundaries produce volcanoes
options.B: No, subduction-related convergent boundaries commonly generate volcanic arcs, but continent-continent collision zones such as the central Himalayas do not generally produce a continuous active volcanic arc like an oceanic subduction margin
options.C: Yes, but only at oceanic-oceanic boundaries
options.D: No, convergent boundaries never produce volcanoes

questions.explanation: No. Subduction-related convergent boundaries commonly generate volcanic arcs, but continent-continent collision zones such as the central Himalayas do not generally produce a continuous active volcanic arc like an oceanic subduction margin.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What type of earthquakes are typical at convergent boundaries?

options.A: Only shallow earthquakes
options.B: Earthquakes from shallow to deep

questions.explanation: Convergent boundaries are associated with earthquakes from shallow to deep, often with volcanic arcs nearby.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a transform plate boundary?

options.A: A plate margin where two plates move away from each other
options.B: A plate margin where two plates slide horizontally past each other; movement is commonly accommodated by strike-slip faults
options.C: A plate margin where two plates move towards each other
options.D: A zone where oceanic lithosphere descends into the mantle

questions.explanation: A transform boundary is a plate margin where two plates slide horizontally past each other. Movement is commonly accommodated by strike-slip faults.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Is crust created or destroyed at transform boundaries?

options.A: Crust is created
options.B: Crust is destroyed
options.C: In the idealised model, transform motion neither creates nor destroys lithosphere; it transfers motion between other plate-boundary segments or accommodates lateral displacement
options.D: Both creation and destruction occur simultaneously

questions.explanation: In the idealised model, transform motion neither creates nor destroys lithosphere. It transfers motion between other plate-boundary segments or accommodates lateral displacement.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What hazards occur at transform boundaries?

options.A: Volcanic eruptions only
options.B: Earthquakes are the main hazard because friction can lock faults, allowing stress to accumulate before sudden rupture

questions.explanation: Earthquakes are the main hazard because friction can lock faults, allowing stress to accumulate before sudden rupture. Transform boundaries do not typically produce the continuous volcanic arcs associated with subduction.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a well-known example of a transform boundary?

options.A: Mid-Atlantic Ridge
options.B: San Andreas Fault system in California

questions.explanation: The San Andreas Fault system in California is a well-known example between the Pacific and North American plate systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Do transform boundaries typically produce volcanic arcs?

options.A: Yes, they produce the same volcanic arcs as subduction zones
options.B: No, transform boundaries do not typically produce the continuous volcanic arcs associated with subduction
options.C: Yes, but only in continental settings
options.D: Yes, but only in oceanic settings

questions.explanation: Transform boundaries do not typically produce the continuous volcanic arcs associated with subduction.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is subduction?

options.A: The process by which new oceanic crust is created at mid-ocean ridges
options.B: The process in which one lithospheric plate, usually oceanic, descends beneath another plate into the mantle at a convergent boundary
options.C: The process by which two plates slide past each other
options.D: The process by which continents move through the ocean

questions.explanation: Subduction is the process in which one lithospheric plate, usually oceanic, descends beneath another plate into the mantle at a convergent boundary.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why does subduction occur?

options.A: Because oceanic plates are less dense than continental plates
options.B: Because older oceanic lithosphere cools, thickens and becomes relatively dense; at a convergent boundary it can sink beneath another plate, helped by gravity and the negative buoyancy of the descending slab
options.C: Because of tidal forces from the Moon
options.D: Because of wind stress on the ocean surface

questions.explanation: Older oceanic lithosphere cools, thickens and becomes relatively dense. At a convergent boundary it can sink beneath another plate, helped by gravity and the negative buoyancy of the descending slab.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the main features of a subduction zone?

options.A: A mid-ocean ridge and rift valley
options.B: A deep-sea trench, a dipping zone of earthquakes called the Wadati-Benioff zone, deformation and accretion of sediments, possible forearc and back-arc regions, and commonly a volcanic arc on the overriding plate
options.C: A strike-slip fault and shallow earthquakes only
options.D: A continental rift and basaltic volcanism

questions.explanation: The main features of a subduction zone include a deep-sea trench, a dipping zone of earthquakes called the Wadati-Benioff zone, deformation and accretion of sediments, possible forearc and back-arc regions, and commonly a volcanic arc on the overriding plate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Wadati-Benioff zone?

options.A: A zone of shallow earthquakes at mid-ocean ridges
options.B: The inclined zone of earthquake foci that traces the descending slab within a subduction zone; earthquakes can occur from shallow depths to several hundred kilometres, reaching about 700 km in some subduction systems
options.C: A zone of volcanic activity at transform boundaries
options.D: The region where new oceanic crust is created

questions.explanation: The Wadati-Benioff zone is the inclined zone of earthquake foci that traces the descending slab within a subduction zone. Earthquakes can occur from shallow depths to several hundred kilometres, reaching about 700 km in some subduction systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why do volcanoes form above many subduction zones?

options.A: Because the entire descending slab melts immediately
options.B: Because water and other volatiles released from the descending slab promote melting in the mantle wedge above it; magma can rise through the overriding plate and form a volcanic arc
options.C: Because of friction between the two plates

questions.explanation: Water and other volatiles released from the descending slab promote melting in the mantle wedge above it. Magma can rise through the overriding plate and form a volcanic arc. The process is not simply because the entire slab melts.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the products of subduction?

options.A: Only new oceanic crust
options.B: Subduction consumes oceanic lithosphere and contributes to trenches, earthquakes, volcanic arcs, mountain belts, metamorphism and recycling of crustal materials into the mantle

questions.explanation: Subduction consumes oceanic lithosphere and contributes to trenches, earthquakes, volcanic arcs, mountain belts, metamorphism and recycling of crustal materials into the mantle.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following regions is associated with subduction systems?

options.A: The Andes
options.B: The East African Rift

questions.explanation: The Andes, Japan, the Aleutian Islands, the Cascades and parts of the Indonesian archipelago are associated with subduction systems, although each region has its own tectonic complexity.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT associated with subduction systems?

options.A: Japan
options.B: The Aleutian Islands

questions.explanation: The East African Rift is a continental divergent boundary, not a subduction system. The Andes, Japan, the Aleutian Islands, the Cascades and parts of the Indonesian archipelago are associated with subduction systems.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is seafloor spreading?

options.A: The process by which oceanic lithosphere descends into the mantle at a convergent boundary
options.B: The process by which new oceanic lithosphere forms at mid-ocean ridges as plates move apart; hot mantle rises, undergoes decompression melting, and magma cools to form new oceanic crust
options.C: The process by which two plates slide past each other
options.D: The process by which continents move through the ocean

questions.explanation: Seafloor spreading is the process by which new oceanic lithosphere forms at mid-ocean ridges as plates move apart. Hot mantle rises, undergoes decompression melting, and magma cools to form new oceanic crust.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Who is strongly associated with the seafloor-spreading hypothesis?

options.A: Alfred Wegener
options.B: Harry Hess

questions.explanation: Harry Hess is strongly associated with the hypothesis, developed in the early 1960s. Robert Dietz also contributed to its development.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the correct sequence of stages in seafloor spreading?

options.A: 1. Plates diverge at a ridge. 2. Hot mantle rises beneath the gap. 3. Pressure decreases and partial melting produces magma. 4. Magma rises and solidifies, forming new oceanic crust. 5. Older oceanic crust moves away from the ridge as newer crust forms
options.B: 1. Plates converge. 2. Oceanic crust subducts. 3. Magma forms. 4. New crust is created at the trench
options.C: 1. Plates slide past each other. 2. Friction melts rock. 3. New crust forms along the fault
options.D: 1. Continents collide. 2. Crust thickens. 3. New oceanic crust forms beneath the mountains

questions.explanation: The main stages of seafloor spreading are: 1. Plates diverge at a ridge. 2. Hot mantle rises beneath the gap. 3. Pressure decreases and partial melting produces magma. 4. Magma rises and solidifies, forming new oceanic crust. 5. Older oceanic crust moves away from the ridge as newer crust forms.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is evidence supporting seafloor spreading?

options.A: Symmetrical magnetic anomaly stripes on both sides of mid-ocean ridges
options.B: The general increase in oceanic crust age away from ridges
options.C: High heat flow near ridge crests and the distribution of ocean-floor sediments

questions.explanation: Evidence supporting seafloor spreading includes symmetrical magnetic anomaly stripes on both sides of mid-ocean ridges, the general increase in oceanic crust age away from ridges, high heat flow near ridge crests, and the distribution of ocean-floor sediments.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are magnetic stripes on the ocean floor?

options.A: Bands of oceanic crust recording alternating normal and reversed geomagnetic polarity as basalt cooled and acquired a magnetic signature; their roughly symmetrical pattern on either side of a ridge supports the formation of new crust and its movement away from the ridge
options.B: Stripes caused by ocean currents
options.C: Bands of sediment deposited by rivers

questions.explanation: Magnetic stripes are bands of oceanic crust recording alternating normal and reversed geomagnetic polarity as basalt cooled and acquired a magnetic signature. Their roughly symmetrical pattern on either side of a ridge supports the formation of new crust and its movement away from the ridge.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why is oceanic crust generally youngest near mid-ocean ridges?

options.A: Because older crust is destroyed at ridges
options.B: Because new crust is formed at the ridge axis and moves away as additional magma solidifies; therefore, the youngest oceanic crust is generally near the ridge, while older crust occurs farther away
options.C: Because sediments accumulate faster near ridges
options.D: Because ridges are located at the centre of oceans

questions.explanation: New crust is formed at the ridge axis and moves away as additional magma solidifies. Therefore, the youngest oceanic crust is generally near the ridge, while older crust occurs farther away.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Does seafloor spreading mean Earth is continuously increasing in size?

options.A: Yes, Earth is expanding continuously
options.B: No, new oceanic lithosphere formed at ridges is balanced over geological time by the destruction or recycling of oceanic lithosphere at subduction zones, so the process does not imply continuous expansion of Earth
options.C: Yes, but only in the Pacific Ocean
options.D: No, because seafloor spreading does not occur

questions.explanation: No. New oceanic lithosphere formed at ridges is balanced over geological time by the destruction or recycling of oceanic lithosphere at subduction zones, so the process does not imply continuous expansion of Earth.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a mid-ocean ridge?

options.A: A long, continuous underwater mountain chain formed mainly at divergent plate boundaries where new oceanic lithosphere is created
options.B: A deep, narrow depression on the ocean floor formed at a convergent boundary
options.C: A strike-slip fault on the ocean floor

questions.explanation: A mid-ocean ridge is a long, continuous underwater mountain chain formed mainly at divergent plate boundaries where new oceanic lithosphere is created.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the characteristics of mid-ocean ridges?

options.A: They are deep, narrow depressions with no volcanic activity
options.B: They form extensive global submarine mountain systems; have elevated ridge crests, central rift valleys in some slower-spreading sections, high heat flow, basaltic volcanism, hydrothermal activity and shallow earthquakes
options.C: They are found only in the Atlantic Ocean
options.D: They are associated with continental collision

questions.explanation: Mid-ocean ridges form extensive global submarine mountain systems; have elevated ridge crests, central rift valleys in some slower-spreading sections, high heat flow, basaltic volcanism, hydrothermal activity and shallow earthquakes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?

options.A: A convergent boundary in the Pacific Ocean
options.B: The divergent plate boundary running through the Atlantic Ocean, separating the North American and Eurasian plates in the north and the South American and African plates in the south

questions.explanation: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the divergent plate boundary running through the Atlantic Ocean, separating the North American and Eurasian plates in the north and the South American and African plates in the south.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is Iceland's relationship to the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?

options.A: Iceland is located far from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
options.B: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and is also influenced by a mantle plume or hotspot; its position makes it an accessible example of an active divergent plate-boundary environment
options.C: Iceland is located on a transform boundary
options.D: Iceland is located on a subduction zone

questions.explanation: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and is also influenced by a mantle plume or hotspot. Its position makes it an accessible example of an active divergent plate-boundary environment.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are all mid-ocean ridges located exactly in the middle of oceans?

options.A: Yes, by definition they must be at the geometric centre of an ocean
options.B: No, the term describes a type of submarine spreading ridge, not a requirement that it lie at the geometric centre of an ocean
options.C: Yes, except for the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
options.D: No, mid-ocean ridges are always located near coastlines

questions.explanation: No. The term describes a type of submarine spreading ridge, not a requirement that it lie at the geometric centre of an ocean.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is an ocean trench?

options.A: A long, continuous underwater mountain chain formed at a divergent boundary
options.B: A long, narrow and very deep depression on the ocean floor, commonly formed at a convergent plate boundary where one plate bends and descends beneath another
options.C: A strike-slip fault on the ocean floor

questions.explanation: An ocean trench is a long, narrow and very deep depression on the ocean floor, commonly formed at a convergent plate boundary where one plate bends and descends beneath another.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the characteristics of ocean trenches?

options.A: They are elevated submarine mountain chains with basaltic volcanism
options.B: They are among the deepest parts of the ocean, are commonly arcuate or curved in plan, and are associated with subduction, powerful earthquakes and volcanic arcs in many regions
options.C: They are associated with continental rifting
options.D: They are formed at transform boundaries

questions.explanation: Ocean trenches are among the deepest parts of the ocean, are commonly arcuate or curved in plan, and are associated with subduction, powerful earthquakes and volcanic arcs in many regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which is the deepest known ocean trench?

options.A: Tonga Trench
options.B: Mariana Trench

questions.explanation: The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific contains the deepest known ocean-floor point, Challenger Deep. Published depth estimates vary with measurement method and survey; commonly cited values are around 10.9 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is Challenger Deep?

options.A: The deepest known ocean-floor point, located in the Mariana Trench
options.B: A mid-ocean ridge in the Atlantic

questions.explanation: The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific contains the deepest known ocean-floor point, Challenger Deep. Published depth estimates vary with measurement method and survey; commonly cited values are around 10.9 kilometres.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How is a trench related to a subduction zone?

options.A: The trench marks the surface expression of the bending and initial descent of the subducting plate; the slab then descends beneath the overriding plate, generating a dipping zone of earthquakes
options.B: The trench is formed by seafloor spreading
options.C: The trench is formed by transform motion
options.D: The trench is unrelated to subduction

questions.explanation: The trench marks the surface expression of the bending and initial descent of the subducting plate. The slab then descends beneath the overriding plate, generating a dipping zone of earthquakes.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following is a major ocean trench?

options.A: Mid-Atlantic Ridge
options.B: Tonga Trench

questions.explanation: Important ocean trenches include the Mariana Trench, Tonga Trench, Japan Trench, Peru-Chile Trench (Atacama Trench), Philippine Trench and Java/Sunda Trench.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which of the following correctly contrasts a mid-ocean ridge with an ocean trench?

options.A: A mid-ocean ridge is associated with divergent boundaries and new lithosphere formation; an ocean trench is associated with convergent/subduction boundaries and lithosphere recycling
options.B: A mid-ocean ridge is a deep depression; an ocean trench is an elevated mountain chain
options.C: Both are associated with divergent boundaries
options.D: Both are associated with transform boundaries

questions.explanation: A mid-ocean ridge is associated with divergent boundaries and new oceanic lithosphere formation; an ocean trench is associated with convergent/subduction boundaries and oceanic lithosphere descent and recycling.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does plate tectonics form mountains?

options.A: Mountain building, or orogeny, commonly occurs where plates converge; compression can fold and fault rock layers, thicken the crust, uplift large regions and generate metamorphism and magmatism
options.B: Mountains form only through volcanic eruptions
options.D: Mountains form only at transform boundaries

questions.explanation: Mountain building, or orogeny, commonly occurs where plates converge. Compression can fold and fault rock layers, thicken the crust, uplift large regions and generate metamorphism and magmatism. Mountains can also form through subduction-related volcanism or fault-block uplift.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are fold mountains?

options.A: Mountains formed by volcanic accumulation
options.B: Mountains that form mainly through compression that bends and shortens rock layers; large fold-and-thrust belts commonly develop at convergent margins

questions.explanation: Fold mountains form mainly through compression that bends and shortens rock layers. Large fold-and-thrust belts commonly develop at convergent margins. The Himalayas are a major example.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Which mountain range is a major example of fold mountains?

options.A: Andes
options.B: Himalayas

questions.explanation: The Himalayas are a major example of fold mountains.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are volcanic mountains?

options.A: Mountains formed by compression and folding
options.B: Mountains that form when erupted lava, ash and other volcanic material accumulate around a vent or along a volcanic system; many form above subduction zones, others occur at hotspots or divergent settings

questions.explanation: Volcanic mountains form when erupted lava, ash and other volcanic material accumulate around a vent or along a volcanic system. Many form above subduction zones; others occur at hotspots or divergent settings.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are fault-block mountains?

options.A: Mountains formed by compression and folding
options.B: Mountains that form when crustal blocks are uplifted, tilted or relatively elevated along faults, commonly under extensional tectonic conditions

questions.explanation: Fault-block mountains form when crustal blocks are uplifted, tilted or relatively elevated along faults, commonly under extensional tectonic conditions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is crustal thickening?

options.A: The thinning of the crust due to extension
options.B: The process that occurs when compression shortens and stacks crustal rocks through folding, thrust faulting and underthrusting; the thicker crust can develop high elevations through isostatic adjustment
options.C: The formation of new oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridges

questions.explanation: Crustal thickening occurs when compression shortens and stacks crustal rocks through folding, thrust faulting and underthrusting. The thicker crust can develop high elevations through isostatic adjustment.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is a fold-and-thrust belt?

options.A: A region of compressed rock layers that have been folded and displaced along thrust faults, commonly forming at convergent plate margins
options.B: A region of new oceanic crust formation

questions.explanation: A fold-and-thrust belt is a region of compressed rock layers that have been folded and displaced along thrust faults, commonly forming at convergent plate margins. The Himalayan foreland and mountain belt include extensive thrust structures.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Are all mountains formed by plate collision?

options.A: Yes, all mountains are formed by continental collision
options.B: No, mountains may form through continental collision, subduction-related volcanism, faulting, volcanic accumulation, uplift and long-term erosion of elevated regions
options.C: No, mountains are only formed by erosion
options.D: Yes, all mountains are formed by subduction

questions.explanation: No. Mountains may form through continental collision, subduction-related volcanism, faulting, volcanic accumulation, uplift and long-term erosion of elevated regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Indian Plate?

options.A: A tectonic plate carrying the Indian subcontinent and adjoining parts of the Indian Ocean lithosphere, moving generally north to north-northeast relative to the Eurasian Plate
options.B: A minor plate located in the Pacific Ocean
options.C: A plate that does not move
options.D: A plate composed only of oceanic crust

questions.explanation: The Indian Plate is a tectonic plate carrying the Indian subcontinent and adjoining parts of the Indian Ocean lithosphere. It moves generally north to north-northeast relative to the Eurasian Plate.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Was the Indian Plate once part of Gondwana?

options.A: No, it was always a separate plate
options.B: Yes, the Indian landmass was part of the southern supercontinent Gondwana; it later separated and moved northward as the intervening oceanic lithosphere was consumed at convergent margins
options.C: Yes, but it was part of Laurasia
options.D: No, it was part of the Pacific Plate

questions.explanation: Yes. The Indian landmass was part of the southern supercontinent Gondwana. It later separated and moved northward as the intervening oceanic lithosphere was consumed at convergent margins.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: In which direction has the Indian Plate moved?

options.A: Southward towards Antarctica
options.B: In broad terms, northward and later north-northeastward towards Eurasia; the exact direction and rate have varied through geological time

questions.explanation: In broad terms, the Indian Plate moved northward and later north-northeastward towards Eurasia. The exact direction and rate have varied through geological time.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How fast does the Indian Plate move today?

options.A: Several metres per year
options.B: On the order of a few centimetres per year, with commonly cited geodetic estimates around 4-5 cm per year relative to Eurasia in parts of the region

questions.explanation: Present-day motion is on the order of a few centimetres per year, with commonly cited geodetic estimates around 4-5 cm per year relative to Eurasia in parts of the region. Rates vary with reference frame, location and tectonic block.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What are the boundaries of the Indian Plate?

options.A: Simple and straight boundaries on all sides
options.B: Complex boundaries: the northern margin is associated with collision and underthrusting beneath Eurasia along the Himalayan region; the western and northwestern margins interact with the Arabian and Eurasian plate systems; the eastern margin is part of a complex subduction and collision zone around the Indo-Burma region; and the southern and southeastern oceanic boundaries include spreading systems in the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: The boundaries of the Indian Plate are complex. The northern margin is associated with collision and underthrusting beneath Eurasia along the Himalayan region; the western and northwestern margins interact with the Arabian and Eurasian plate systems; the eastern margin is part of a complex subduction and collision zone around the Indo-Burma region; and the southern and southeastern oceanic boundaries include spreading systems in the Indian Ocean.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Is the Indian Plate identical to the Indo-Australian Plate?

options.A: Yes, they are always the same
options.B: Not in all modern tectonic models; some school-level maps group India and Australia into the Indo-Australian Plate, but many modern studies distinguish the Indian and Australian plates, with distributed deformation between them in the Indian Ocean
options.C: No, the Indian Plate does not exist
options.D: Yes, because India and Australia move together as one rigid block

questions.explanation: Not in all modern tectonic models. Some school-level maps group India and Australia into the Indo-Australian Plate. Many modern studies distinguish the Indian and Australian plates, with distributed deformation between them in the Indian Ocean.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the significance of the Indian Plate?

options.A: It has no significant geological features
options.B: Its northward movement and collision with Eurasia produced the Himalayan orogen and contributed to uplift of the Tibetan Plateau; its interactions also influence earthquakes in the Himalayas and surrounding regions
options.C: It is the largest tectonic plate

questions.explanation: Its northward movement and collision with Eurasia produced the Himalayan orogen and contributed to uplift of the Tibetan Plateau. Its interactions also influence earthquakes in the Himalayas and surrounding regions.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the Eurasian Plate?

options.A: A major lithospheric plate carrying most of Europe and a large part of Asia; its southern boundary is tectonically complex, involving collision and subduction systems from the Mediterranean region through the Middle East and Himalayas to Southeast Asia
options.B: A minor plate located in the Pacific Ocean
options.C: A plate composed only of oceanic crust
options.D: A plate that does not move

questions.explanation: The Eurasian Plate is a major lithospheric plate carrying most of Europe and a large part of Asia. Its southern boundary is tectonically complex, involving collision and subduction systems from the Mediterranean region through the Middle East and Himalayas to Southeast Asia.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How does the Eurasian Plate interact with the Indian Plate?

options.A: They move apart at a divergent boundary
options.B: The Indian Plate moves northward and underthrusts the Eurasian Plate along the Himalayan collision zone; their convergence shortens and thickens crust, producing the Himalayas and contributing to the Tibetan Plateau
options.C: They slide past each other at a transform boundary

questions.explanation: The Indian Plate moves northward and underthrusts the Eurasian Plate along the Himalayan collision zone. Their convergence shortens and thickens crust, producing the Himalayas and contributing to the Tibetan Plateau.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Does the Eurasian Plate consist only of continental crust?

options.A: Yes, it is entirely continental
options.B: No, it includes extensive continental lithosphere and adjacent oceanic lithosphere in some regions; a tectonic plate is defined by the lithosphere it contains, not simply by a continent
options.D: No, it is composed only of the asthenosphere

questions.explanation: No. It includes extensive continental lithosphere and adjacent oceanic lithosphere in some regions. A tectonic plate is defined by the lithosphere it contains, not simply by a continent.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What happened when the Indian Plate collided with the Eurasian Plate?

options.A: The Indian Plate immediately sank deep into the mantle
options.B: As the Indian Plate moved northward, the oceanic lithosphere of the Neo-Tethys Ocean between India and Eurasia was progressively consumed by subduction; eventually, continental collision occurred, and the Indian continental lithosphere underthrusts Eurasia, causing compression, folding, thrusting, crustal thickening and uplift
options.D: The Indian Plate stopped moving completely

questions.explanation: As the Indian Plate moved northward, the oceanic lithosphere of the Neo-Tethys Ocean between India and Eurasia was progressively consumed by subduction. Eventually, continental collision occurred. The Indian continental lithosphere underthrusts Eurasia, causing compression, folding, thrusting, crustal thickening and uplift.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What was the Neo-Tethys Ocean?

options.A: The oceanic basin that separated the Indian/Gondwanan margin from Eurasia before the India-Asia collision; its oceanic lithosphere was progressively consumed during convergence
options.B: A modern ocean located between India and Australia
options.C: An ancient ocean located between North America and Europe
options.D: A lake that existed in the Himalayas

questions.explanation: The Neo-Tethys Ocean was the oceanic basin that separated the Indian/Gondwanan margin from Eurasia before the India-Asia collision. Its oceanic lithosphere was progressively consumed during convergence.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why did the Indian Plate not simply sink beneath Eurasia like an oceanic plate?

options.A: Because the Indian Plate is made of oceanic crust
options.B: Because continental crust is relatively buoyant and resists deep subduction; when the Indian continental margin reached the Eurasian margin after oceanic lithosphere had been consumed, the collision produced shortening, underthrusting and crustal thickening rather than simple continued oceanic-style subduction
options.C: Because the Eurasian Plate is less dense than the Indian Plate
options.D: Because the Indian Plate is stationary

questions.explanation: Continental crust is relatively buoyant and resists deep subduction. When the Indian continental margin reached the Eurasian margin after oceanic lithosphere had been consumed, the collision produced shortening, underthrusting and crustal thickening rather than simple continued oceanic-style subduction.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What geological structures formed due to the India-Eurasia collision?

options.A: A major fold-and-thrust belt, the Himalayan mountain chain, the Tibetan Plateau, large fault systems and zones of intense seismicity
options.B: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge

questions.explanation: A major fold-and-thrust belt, the Himalayan mountain chain, the Tibetan Plateau, large fault systems and zones of intense seismicity formed due to the collision. The collision also caused widespread metamorphism and magmatism in parts of the broader region.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Is the Indian Plate still moving towards Eurasia?

options.A: No, it has stopped completely
options.B: Yes, convergence continues today, although motion is distributed across the collision zone and surrounding tectonic blocks; this continuing convergence contributes to ongoing deformation and earthquake hazard
options.C: No, it is now moving southward

questions.explanation: Yes. Convergence continues today, although motion is distributed across the collision zone and surrounding tectonic blocks. This continuing convergence contributes to ongoing deformation and earthquake hazard.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why are earthquakes common in the Himalayan region?

options.A: Because of volcanic activity
options.B: Because the Indian Plate continues to converge with and underthrust the Eurasian Plate; stress accumulates along faults and thrust systems, and sudden slip releases energy as earthquakes

questions.explanation: The Indian Plate continues to converge with and underthrust the Eurasian Plate. Stress accumulates along faults and thrust systems; sudden slip releases energy as earthquakes. The region is therefore seismically active.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: When did the main India-Asia collision commonly thought to occur in school-level accounts?

options.A: Around 500 million years ago
options.B: Around 50 million years ago (early Cenozoic)

questions.explanation: School-level accounts commonly place the main collision in the early Cenozoic, around 50 million years ago, but estimates vary. The exact timing of initial contact and subsequent stages is an active research subject.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: How were the Himalayas formed?

options.A: Through volcanic eruptions only
options.B: Mainly through the northward movement of the Indian Plate and its collision with the Eurasian Plate after the intervening Neo-Tethys oceanic lithosphere was largely consumed by subduction; compression caused folding, thrust faulting, crustal shortening and thickening, leading to uplift of the mountain belt

questions.explanation: The Himalayas formed mainly through the northward movement of the Indian Plate and its collision with the Eurasian Plate after the intervening Neo-Tethys oceanic lithosphere was largely consumed by subduction. Compression caused folding, thrust faulting, crustal shortening and thickening, leading to uplift of the mountain belt.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: What is the correct sequence of stages in the formation of the Himalayas?

options.A: 1. India was part of Gondwana. 2. The Indian landmass separated and moved northward. 3. Neo-Tethys oceanic lithosphere between India and Eurasia was subducted. 4. India collided with Eurasia. 5. Continued convergence caused underthrusting, folding, thrusting and crustal thickening. 6. Uplift and erosion continue to shape the Himalayas
options.B: 1. India collided with Eurasia. 2. Neo-Tethys subducted. 3. India separated from Gondwana
options.C: 1. Neo-Tethys subducted. 2. India separated from Gondwana. 3. India collided with Eurasia. 4. India moved northward
options.D: 1. India moved northward. 2. India collided with Eurasia. 3. India separated from Gondwana. 4. Neo-Tethys subducted

questions.explanation: The sequence is: 1. India was part of Gondwana. 2. The Indian landmass separated and moved northward. 3. Neo-Tethys oceanic lithosphere between India and Eurasia was subducted. 4. India collided with Eurasia. 5. Continued convergence caused underthrusting, folding, thrusting and crustal thickening. 6. Uplift and erosion continue to shape the Himalayas.

questions.subject: Geography
questions.question: Why are the Himalayas called young fold mountains?

options.A: Because they are geologically young compared with ancient mountain systems and were formed largely by folding, thrusting and crustal thickening during the ongoing India-Eurasia collision
options.B: Because they are the oldest mountains on Earth
options.C: Because they are made of young volcanic rocks
